thread.title: Apple and the VA may bring electronic health records to 9M veterans (AAPL)

author: Nicky Lineaweaver
title: Apple and the VA may bring electronic health records to 9M veterans (AAPL)

organizations.name: business insider intelligence " digital health brie

text:
This story was delivered to Business Insider Intelligence " Digital Health Briefing " subscribers hours before appearing on Business Insider. To be the first to know, please click here .
Apple is in preliminary talks with the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to provide portable electronic health records (EHRs) to veterans of the US military, which would enable the tech giant to carve out a significant chunk of the EHR market, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Business Insider Intelligence The partnership would likely build on Health Records , a feature of the iOS Health app that enables iPhone users to view, store, and access their health data from disparate sources in a single location. The pair also aims to let veterans find a variety of healthcare facilities near them using geotagging features, quickly share their test results, and track prescriptions.
Landing a partnership with the VA could accelerate Apple's push to make Health Records a staple in US healthcare:
Apple could tap into the VA's large pool of enrolled members. Providing a personal EHR solution to the 9 million veterans enrolled in the VA would make Health Records the largest mobile platform for storing records on personal phones, cofounder of Impathiq, a health data analytics company, told The Wall Street Journal. Moreover, Apple's also discussed offering solutions to active-duty troops, which would potentially give Apple access to more than 1 million additional individuals. And the VA could provide Apple with a launching point to scale Health Records to the rest of the healthcare industry. Currently, Health Records is only supported by 75 health firms. But if the VA pushes its enrollees to adopt Health Records, the healthcare institutions that serve VA members nationwide would likely have to follow suit, making it easier for Apple to scale its platform to non-VA consumers. An improved EHR solution would be in high demand, as industry players are scrambling to address a lack of data interoperability. Nearly half of US doctors think EHRs detract from their clinical effectiveness, and only 8% of doctors see a clinically-related benefit from their EHR system.
Moreover, just 20% of US health systems use EHR data from outside sources, contributing to unnecessary duplicate tests — so it's unsurprising that C-suite level health system executives recently pegged poor interoperability as a top concern for 2019.
And Apple's not the only player looking into new proprietary EHR solutions to address inefficiencies — insurance company UnitedHealth Group plans to launch a fully portable individual health record in 2019, according to MedCity News.
